titre: *L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat* (The Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat Station) Sparked No Panic
accroche: The film accused of terrifying the very first movie audience was shot a year and a half after that supposed panic.
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 28, 1895, at the Grand Café on boulevard des Capucines in Paris, the Lumière brothers give the first paid public screening of their Cinématographe. Legend has it that a train rushing straight at the camera then sowed panic in the room: spectators supposedly screamed, leapt to their feet, and some even fled toward the back of the room, convinced the locomotive was about to burst out of the screen. The film associated with this scene has a precise name in the Lumière catalog, film no. 653, *Arrivée d'un train à La Ciotat*.

## A train shot a year and a half too late

The official catalog of the Institut Lumière, which holds all of the original films, nevertheless places the shooting of this particular film in the summer of 1897, a year and a half after the Grand Café screening. The historians Michelle Aubert and Jean-Claude Seguin established that date from the ages of the Lumière children visible at the edge of the frame, including little Joséphine Lumière, recognizable by her tartan cape. The program of the ten films shown on December 28, 1895, moreover mentions no train arrival: film no. 653 therefore could not physically have been on it. Another version, shot at the very beginning of 1896 and since found in the Lumière archives, may have been shown in Lyon in late January of that year, but nothing links that screening to any panic either.

There remains the question of the panic itself, regardless of the date. The film historian Martin Loiperdinger searched the press and police archives of the time for the slightest trace of such a commotion. He found none. In his view, the anecdote of an audience so terrified it fled belongs to historical fantasy, repeated without checking by film historians long after the fact, such as Erik Barnouw in 1974. The text closest to the events remains an article by the Russian journalist Maxim Gorky, published in 1896 after he discovered the Cinématographe at the Nizhny Novgorod fair: in it he describes his own fright before the image of a train, ready, he says, to reduce him to a “ripped sack of mangled flesh and broken bones.” But that text, a personal reflection on illusion, describes no stampede, no collective scream, no injured person in the room.

## What this changes

The film presented today as proof of the naivety of cinema's very first audience therefore could not have produced the effect attributed to it: it did not yet exist on the evening that effect is supposed to have occurred. The anecdote survives nonetheless, because it tells a story flattering to cinema itself, that of an art so powerful from birth that it would abolish at a stroke the boundary between image and reality. Loiperdinger calls this, in his own article, cinema's “founding myth”: a story that ultimately says less about the 1895 audience than about what cinema has always wanted to believe about its own power.

citation.texte: Contemporary reports of panic reactions among the audience cannot be found. The repeatedly reiterated anecdote that the contemporary audience felt physically threatened and therefore panicked must be relegated to the realm of historical fantasy.
citation.source: The Moving Image, vol. 4, no. 1, 2004, quoted by the International Documentary Association

carte.punch: The train said to have terrified cinema's first audience was filmed a year and a half later.
carte.idee: The film associated with the panic of cinema's first audience, in 1895, was actually shot in the summer of 1897, according to the Institut Lumière catalog. No period account, from police or press, reports any real panic that evening either.

quiz.question: What does the Institut Lumière catalog reveal about film no. 653, the film associated with the myth of the 1895 panic?
choix: The train seen entering the station never existed; the film was a late photomontage
The film was screened before it had even been developed, which explains an image judged frightening
The film was shot in the summer of 1897, a year and a half after the December 28, 1895 screening with which it is associated
The film actually shows a Paris station repainted to look like the one at La Ciotat
quiz.explication: The historians Michelle Aubert and Jean-Claude Seguin dated the shooting of film no. 653 to the summer of 1897, based on the ages of the Lumière children visible in the frame. The film therefore could not have been shown at the Grand Café in December 1895. The other three options are made up.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the program of the ten films shown on December 28, 1895, at the Grand Café show?
choix: It does include a train arrival, but shown dead last
It includes two different versions of a train arrival
It mentions only scenes shot in Paris
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The program of the ten films shown that evening mentions no train arrival, which confirms, independently of the 1897 dating, that film no. 653 could not have been on it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the historians Aubert and Seguin rely on to date the shooting of film no. 653 to the summer of 1897?
choix: Weather records matching the lighting visible on the film stock
Accounting documents from the La Ciotat station
The ages of the Lumière children visible at the edge of the frame, including little Joséphine
A letter from Louis Lumière giving the exact date of the shoot
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Aubert and Seguin established the shooting date from the ages of the Lumière children visible at the edge of the frame, including little Joséphine Lumière, recognizable by her tartan cape.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the historian Martin Loiperdinger find when he searched the press and police archives of the time for a trace of the supposed panic?
choix: Several consistent accounts from terrified spectators
A single police report mentioning minor injuries
Press clippings mentioning a harmless jostling
No trace at all, the anecdote being, in his view, historical fantasy
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Loiperdinger found no contemporary trace of panic in the press or police archives, and concludes that the anecdote belongs to historical fantasy repeated without checking.
